source_tier: Mixed. Heyerdahl's own statements are in a popular magazine (Azerbaijan International, an English-language magazine about Azerbaijan published from Los Angeles and Baku): primary for what he claimed, popular tier for evidential weight, and he was not a trained archaeologist. Sigari 2017 and Farajova 2023 are peer-reviewed. Farajova 2012 is a conference proceedings paper; the dissertation abstract is an institutional document. Helskog 2014 is a chapter in an edited academic volume from a Norwegian scholarly publisher, arising from a conference co-organised by universities in Azerbaijan and Norway. Kelder 2023 is a peer-reviewed society proceedings journal, used here only as a secondary witness to one page of Helskog.
access_status: Fully read: the five Azerbaijan International articles (downloaded as HTML and read as text); Farajova 2023 (all 10 pages, publisher PDF); Farajova 2012 (14 pages); the 2011 conference programme including Helskog's abstract; Kelder 2023 (searched in full for Gobustan, Caspian and Helskog). Partly read: Sigari 2017, pp. 59-61 opened directly as page previews for the typology and Rock 29 passages (a sibling research file in this folder, Sigari_2017_boat_engravings.json, records a full read by another agent). Farajova's dissertation abstract was text-searched for boats, Helskog and Heyerdahl, not read end to end. NOT read: Helskog's 2014 chapter. ResearchGate returned 403 or 'temporarily unavailable', Google Books has no record for the ISBN, no Munin or Academia copy was found, and the book is sold in print only. Farajova's chapter in the same volume ('Boats in Rock Art of Gobustan', pp. 191-201) and her 2011 Adoranten article were also not found online. Farajova 2018 (Quaternary International 491, the Firuz 2 paper) was blocked. No browser was available for the blocked pages (Playwright's browser is not installed on this machine).
author_credentials: Thor Heyerdahl (1914-2002): Norwegian explorer, trained at Oslo in biology and geography ('I had been educated in Oslo University in biology', AI 8.2); no archaeological fieldwork at Gobustan, only visits. The magazine gives inconsistent visit years: 1980, 1994, 1999 and 2000 (AI 14.4); 1989 and 1994 (AI 6.2); Heyerdahl himself says 'The first time I came to Azerbaijan was in 1981' (AI 8.2), and the Roggen volume's contents list also has 1981, 1994, 1999, 2000. Knut Helskog: Professor, Tromsø University Museum (as titled in the 2011 programme), specialist on the Alta rock art in Arctic Norway; visited Gobustan (co-author with Anne-Sophie Hygen of a 2006 advisory mission report on the Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape, cited in Farajova's reference lists, and presented at the rocks during the 2011 conference). Dario Sigari: rock art archaeologist, fieldwork at Gobustan from 2015. Malahat Farajova: former director of the Gobustan reserve, decades of fieldwork there; Azerbaijan State University of Culture and Arts in 2023. Jorrit Kelder: Aegean and Near Eastern archaeologist, Leiden; no Gobustan fieldwork.

exact_quotes.location: Heyerdahl, AI 3.1 (1995), section 'Identical Petroglyphs in Norway and Azerbaijan'
exact_quotes.quote: It may not be pure coincidence that the ship petroglyphs that the early Azeri depicted while navigating on the Caspian Sea and up the Russian rivers are identical to those of the ancestors of the Vikings along the fjords of Norway millennia later. In Scandinavia, there are two different types of boat petroglyphs, both well represented in Norway. One is similar to those at Gobustan and is drawn as a simple sickle-shaped line which forms the base of the ship with vertical lines on deck to illustrate crew or raised oars.

exact_quotes.location: Heyerdahl, AI 3.1 (1995), section 'Oral Tradition or Fairy Tale?'
exact_quotes.quote: I suspect that the present Azeri people and the Aser of the Norse sagas have common roots and that my ancestry originated there.

My growing suspicion is that what today is left as the little Republic of Azerbaijan around the capital Baku is only vestiges of what was once a large and dynamic nation bordering on an inland sea but transmitting merchandise and even colonists to remote outposts in both Asia and Europe.

And that's when I became interested in the fact that you have two types of boat petroglyphs in Gobustan. On my first visit, I came to study the reed ships that are similar to the boats of the ancient Mediterranean.

exact_quotes.location: Heyerdahl, AI 8.2 (2000), on the Roman inscription and Snorri
exact_quotes.quote: If this inscription matched Snorre's record, it would mean that Odin left for Scandinavia during the second half of the 1st century AD.

exact_quotes.location: AI 8.2 (2000), photo caption (the magazine's words, not Heyerdahl's)
exact_quotes.quote: In the ancient caves of Gobustan which date back at least 5,000 years, cave drawings depict two different kinds of boats that were used for early navigation. Heyerdahl is convinced that people living in the area now known as Azerbaijan settled in Scandinavia around 100 AD.
He noted that the boats drawn at Gobustan featured the sun at the front of the boat, rather than at the back.
It was a concept that came under heavy criticism in Norway. But to the end, Heyerdahl did not back off, though it has yet to be proven.

There are boats that possess a prow or stern. The prows are characteristically engraved in a hooked shape. Accompanying these ships are sun-like symbols that can be set at the end of the prow line or can be realised by curving the prow and adding the rays. On the other hand, both sterns and prows can be curved towards the deck. All these stylistically different boats can appear on the same rock, possibly revealing a relative chronology among them (see Rock No. 8).

The keel can be flat (see Rock No. 29 northern face-eastern section, Rock No. 41) or curved (see Rock No. 8). The deck may be differentiated by the way of depicting the so called crew of the ship. This attachment can be depicted as simple, small vertical segmented lines (see Rocks No. 29, 30, 765A, 41, 42), or as "X"-shaped elements (see Rocks [unnumbered] and Rock No. 8).

The prow is oriented eastwards, towards the Caspian Sea, and is decorated with a sun-shaped symbol. Concerning its relationship with the other figures, the boat overlaps both a zoomorph and two male anthropomorphs.
It is quite likely that the most ancient means of transportation for the inhabitants of Gobustan were boats depicted 7800 years ago, which could accommodate more than 50 people.
the petroglyphs on the southern side of stone 29 on the upper terrace of Mount Boyukdash are very important. Of particular interest is the plot with boats, and hunters armed with bows and arrows.

A bright series of petroglyphs from the third period are images of boats. They are represented in almost all the sites of Gobustan. Boat petroglyphs are localized mainly on the rocks of the Beyukdash and Kichikdash mountains. If in the second stage of the I Mesolithic period, only hunters with bows and arrows are represented, then in the third period the meaning of the plot changes: images of boats are presented in the center, and hunters of the second period with bows and arrows around them. In the fourth period, figures of people appear around the boats with their hands up, as if berthing boats to the shore.
Late Neolithic period (VII-IV millenina BC) – Images of aurochs, boats and small images of archers.

exact_quotes.location: Helskog, abstract in the 2011 Baku conference programme, pp. 11-12
exact_quotes.quote: The first uses of boats are believed to have occurred 10000 - 11000 years ago, and most likely there were multiple points of origin rather than one. In Scandinavia the oldest indications of crossing coastal waters are from approximately 10000 – 9000 years ago. Boats are depicted in 7000 - 6000 years old petroglyphs, which might be younger or older than the oldest boats depicted in Gobustan. – The discussion will examine the figures and contexts they are a part of, to illuminate the similarities and differences of the early cultural and maritime environments in two regions far apart.

exact_quotes.location: Kelder 2023, p. 152, footnote 13 (a secondary report of Helskog 2014, p. 211)
exact_quotes.quote: Farajova 2012; earlier dates, suggesting a date of 14,000 to 11,000 BC seem to have been based on assumptions (e.g., that the sea-level must have reached the caves where the boat-petroglyphs were carved) or on extremely problematic stylistic considerations (Sagona 2018: 73-75; Helskog 2014: 211).

exact_quotes.location: Novus publisher's description of the Roggen volume
exact_quotes.quote: The forum was a cooperative effort between universities in Azerbaijan and Norway and served as a catalyst in the creation of this book, which documents much of the research to date related to Heyerdahl's theory – both supportive, as well as critical, of it.

key_claims: Heyerdahl (1995): the Gobustan ship petroglyphs are 'identical' to those of 'the ancestors of the Vikings' in Norway, made 'millennia later'. The likeness he names is one shape: a simple sickle-shaped hull line with vertical strokes on deck for crew or raised oars.

Heyerdahl (1995, 2000): from that likeness, plus Snorri Sturluson's account of Odin coming from the land of the 'Aser' east of the Black Sea and the name 'Azeri', he suspects Scandinavians descend from people of what is now Azerbaijan. He presents it as a 'growing suspicion' in 1995 and as near-proof by 2000 ('there can no longer be any doubt').

Heyerdahl dates the supposed migration to the second half of the 1st century AD, using the Roman inscription at Gobustan (he puts it between AD 84 and 97) and 31 generations of kings at 25 years each. The 'around 100 AD' figure repeated online comes from a magazine photo caption.

Heyerdahl says Gobustan has 'two types of boat petroglyphs': reed ships like those of the ancient Mediterranean, and (by implication from the 1995 article, where the two types are said of Scandinavia) a second type he links to skin boats and Odin's folding ship. He never describes the second Gobustan type.
The sun-at-the-prow observation is attributed to Heyerdahl by the magazine (1998), not stated by him in the two articles under his name.

Sigari (2017) gives the only published descriptive typology found: long boats over 1.50 m and shorter ones; flat or curved keels; crew as short vertical strokes or as X-shaped elements; prows 'characteristically engraved in a hooked shape'; sun-like symbols either set at the end of the prow line or made by curving the prow and adding rays; and 'both sterns and prows can be curved towards the deck'.

On that description, a raised, hooked or curved end is the normal form of a Gobustan boat, not an exception, and the sun-prow is a recurring type. Sigari et al. 2025 (sibling result) says the same of the later phase: 'the prows are curved and the solar symbol becomes a recurrent feature'.
The boat on the south face of Rock 29 is itself a sun-prow boat (Sigari 2017, p. 59), so its 'raised terminal' belongs to a known local type.

Farajova puts boats in her Neolithic period (7th millennium BC onward; 'depicted 7800 years ago'), says they occur at almost all Gobustan sites, and describes a recurring arrangement of boats in the centre with bow-and-arrow hunters around them. She names the south side of stone 29 as a 'plot with boats, and hunters armed with bows and arrows'.

Helskog (2011 abstract): the oldest Scandinavian boat petroglyphs are 7,000 to 6,000 years old and 'might be younger or older than the oldest boats depicted in Gobustan'; boats probably had 'multiple points of origin rather than one'; his aim was to compare 'similarities and differences' between 'two regions far apart'.

[uncertain] Helskog (2014 chapter): its argument and conclusion could not be read. The one point confirmed at second hand is that p. 211 is cited by Kelder for doubt about the 14,000 to 11,000 BC dates for Gobustan boats. Whether Helskog rejects, qualifies or accepts a Caspian-Scandinavia link is not established here.
evidence_offered: Heyerdahl: visual resemblance between one boat shape at Gobustan and one of two boat shapes in Norwegian rock art; Snorri's 13th-century Ynglinga saga prologue; the name similarity Aser/Azeri; Herodotus on skin boats in Armenia; the Roman legionary inscription at Gobustan; a generation count. No tracings, measurements, counts, dates for the carvings or comparison of specific panels. Sigari: field recording of nine boat-bearing rocks in July 2015, superimpositions and terrace altitude. Farajova: 3D modelling and night photography of the panels, radiocarbon dates from cave deposits. Helskog: [uncertain] not read; the abstract promises comparison of figures and their contexts.

boat_motif: Heyerdahl: gives no date for the Gobustan boats. He says the Norwegian ones were made 'millennia later' (AI 3.1). The magazine supplies 'at least 5,000 years' for the caves (AI 8.2, 14.4) and '12-8th century B.C.' for the oldest petroglyphs (AI 6.2); these conflict with each other and with the specialists.

Sigari 2017: first boats on the upper terraces 16 to 14 ka 'or even before'; Rock 8 boats 14 to 12 ka cal BP 'or to a later one'; sun symbol and X-shaped crew arrive after that. No absolute date for the sun-prow type.

Farajova 2012: boats in the 'Late Neolithic period (VII-IV millennia BC)'. Farajova 2023: boats 'depicted 7800 years ago'. Dissertation abstract: boats are a feature of Period III, Neolithic, from 7000 BC.
Helskog 2011 abstract: Scandinavian boat petroglyphs 7,000 to 6,000 years old; no figure for Gobustan, only that its oldest boats may be older or younger than that.
Kelder 2023: 'at least some' Gobustan boats 'likely' date to the 7th to 4th millennium BC; the 14,000 to 11,000 BC dates rest on assumptions (citing Sagona 2018 and Helskog 2014: 211).
site_or_layers: Farajova 2023 periodisation of Gobustan rock art: Period I about 14,000 BP; Neolithic 9000-7800 BP; Chalcolithic 7000-6000 BP; Bronze Age 4th to late 2nd millennia BC. Ana Zaga radiocarbon groups run from 9170 ± 40 BP to 1560 ± 55 BP.
Roman inscription at Gobustan: Heyerdahl says after AD 84 and before AD 97.
supposed_migration: Heyerdahl: second half of the 1st century AD (magazine caption: 'around 100 AD').

dating_method: None of these sources dates a boat carving directly. Heyerdahl uses no dating method for the carvings at all; his one date is for a migration and comes from a Roman inscription plus a generation count on saga king lists. Sigari: style, superimposition and shoreline correlation with Caspian high stands. Farajova: style plus radiocarbon dates from cave layers, on the rule that carvings 'precede or are contemporaneous with' a layer that covers them. Helskog's known method at Alta is shoreline displacement; [uncertain] what he applied to Gobustan in 2014 is not confirmed beyond Kelder's report that p. 211 treats the sea-level argument for very early dates as an assumption.
panel_details: Typology across the corpus (Sigari 2017, p. 59, nine rocks: Böyük Daş Rocks 29, 30, 765A, 41, 42, two unnumbered, Rock 8; Kiçik Daş Rock 19): long boats over 1.50 m (Rocks 29, 30, 765A, 41) and shorter boats (Rocks 42, 8, unnumbered); keel flat (Rock 29 north face east section, Rock 41) or curved (Rock 8); crew as vertical strokes (Rocks 29, 30, 765A, 41, 42) or X-shapes (unnumbered, Rock 8); hooked prows; sun symbol at the prow end or formed from a curved prow with rays; sterns and prows may both curve towards the deck; different styles can share one rock. Rock 29, south face: one boat on a natural curved crack, prow east towards the Caspian with a sun-shaped symbol, overlapping a zoomorph and two male anthropomorphs. Farajova 2023 calls the same face a 'plot with boats, and hunters armed with bows and arrows' and reports 38 newly found images there, including 'indeterminate lines and marks under the image of a boat' recorded by Rustamov, and a boat fragment that 'crosses the anthropomorphic figure'. Rock 29 east face (Farajova 2023): 40 new images including 10 boats, 9 anthropomorphs, 5 zoomorphs, and lines running down from cup-like hollows through hunter figures. Rock 19, Kiçik Daş (Firuz 2): 7 and 10 further boats found in 2014 (Farajova, Valcamonica paper). Heyerdahl names no rock or panel.
geographic_claims: Heyerdahl: Caspian Sea, then 'up the river Volga which was navigable past present-day Moscow to its sources', which lie 'suspiciously close to the sources of the river Dvina which empties into the Baltic Sea at Riga'. Odin's route in Snorri as he reads it: 'northwestwardly through Russia, Saxland, and Denmark into Sweden'. He also has Azerbaijani merchants trading by skin boat with Babylonia. He places the land of the Aser 'east of the Caucasus mountains and the Black Sea' but proposes no Black Sea, Kura or Phasis route and never mentions Greece, Colchis or the Argonauts. Sigari and Farajova: Caspian only. Helskog: coastal Scandinavia and the Caspian compared as 'two regions far apart'.
counter_evidence: The shape Heyerdahl relies on is generic. A curved hull line with vertical strokes for crew is about the simplest way to draw a manned boat, and he himself says he saw the same 'sickle-shaped ships' on Easter Island, in Egypt and in Mesopotamia (AI 8.2). A likeness found everywhere cannot single out one link.

His dates do not meet. He has the Norwegian carvings 'millennia later' than Gobustan's, yet puts the migration in the 1st century AD. Specialists place Gobustan boats in the Neolithic or earlier (Farajova) or the late Pleistocene to early Holocene (Sigari), thousands of years before any 1st-century movement; Helskog's abstract puts Scandinavian boat carvings at 7,000 to 6,000 years old, also long before it.
Helskog's abstract says boats 'most likely' had 'multiple points of origin rather than one', which cuts against deriving one region's boats from the other.
The magazine that published Heyerdahl records that the idea 'came under heavy criticism in Norway' and 'has yet to be proven' (AI 14.4).

For the Argonaut proposal: the 'unusual raised terminal' is not unusual at Gobustan. Hooked prows are 'characteristic', both ends can curve up, and the sun-prow recurs on Rocks 8, 19 and 29. A feature shared by many local boats cannot mark one carving as a particular ship.
Boats with armed men around them are also a stock arrangement: Farajova describes boats in the centre with bow-and-arrow hunters around them as the pattern of a whole period.
On Rock 29's south face the boat overlaps two male figures (Sigari), so boat and figures were not cut at one time.
independent_corroboration: For Heyerdahl's Azerbaijan-Scandinavia claim: none found from a rock art specialist. The Roggen volume is described by its publisher as containing work 'both supportive, as well as critical'; [uncertain] which chapters are which was not checked, since none could be opened. Sigari et al. 2025 notes only that 'some connections have already been proposed' with Scandinavian figures, without endorsing them. For the typology: Sigari's description is consistent with Farajova's and with Sigari et al. 2025; the sun-at-the-prow feature is reported independently by the magazine (1998), Sigari (2017) and Sigari et al. (2025).
alternative_explanations: The resemblance between Gobustan and Scandinavian boats is read by specialists as convergence: two coastal peoples drawing the craft they depended on, in the most economical form. Helskog's abstract frames boats in both regions as tied to 'transportation, fishing and hunting' and to 'symbolism, beliefs and ritual communication', and looks at differences as well as similarities. At Gobustan the boats are read locally: a record of life beside a higher Caspian (Sigari), or a means of transport for Neolithic communities, shown with hunters in recurring scenes (Farajova). The sun on the prow is treated as a decorative or symbolic convention of a later boat style, not as the emblem of one vessel. Heyerdahl's 'reed boat' identification is his own; neither Sigari nor Farajova in the texts read says what the boats were made of.
verification_status: Checked against the opened Azerbaijan International pages: every Heyerdahl quotation; the 'sickle-shaped line' description; 'two types' of boats; the Volga-Dvina route; the AD 84-97 inscription argument; the '100 AD' caption; the sun-at-the-front remark (attributed, in AI 6.2); 'heavy criticism in Norway' (AI 14.4); the conflicting visit years.

Checked against Sigari 2017 p. 59 opened directly: the typology wording, hooked prows, sun symbol, sterns and prows curved towards the deck, Rock 29 south-face boat with sun-shaped prow overlapping two male figures.
Checked against the opened Farajova 2023 PDF: 'boats depicted 7800 years ago', the south side of stone 29 as boats with bow-and-arrow hunters, 10 boats on the east side, periodisation.
Checked against the opened dissertation abstract: boats at almost all sites, boats-in-centre with hunters around; that it cites Helskog 2014 with pp. 202-219.
Checked against the opened conference programme: Helskog's 2011 title and abstract, quoted in full above.
Checked against the publisher's page: the 2014 volume's title, editor, ISBN, contents list and that Helskog's chapter starts at p. 202 and Farajova's at p. 191.

NOT checked: anything Helskog says in the 2014 chapter. The statement about p. 211 is Kelder's report, read in Kelder, not in Helskog. Kelder gives the chapter's pages as 201-219; the publisher's contents and Farajova give 202.

NOT checked: Heyerdahl's book (Ingen grenser, 1999, and Jakten på Odin, 2001, with Per Lillieström); Farajova's chapter in the Roggen volume; Farajova 2011 in Adoranten; Farajova 2018 in Quaternary International; Djafarsade 1973 for boat counts.

A search summary attributed an abstract about 'maritime warriors' and 'maritime polities in Scandinavia' to Helskog's chapter. That wording matches other authors' work on Scandinavian ship carvings and was not found on any page opened. Do not use it.
relevance_to_essay: Two uses. First, the typology undercuts the proposal's 'unusual raised terminal': hooked and upcurved ends are standard on Gobustan boats and the Rock 29 south-face boat is an ordinary sun-prow type, shown with the armed figures that commonly accompany boats there. Second, Heyerdahl is the precedent. A famous outsider saw a likeness in the same boats, tied it to a much later written legend (Snorri's Odin) and announced an origin. The parallel with reading Rock 29 as the Argo is close, and the published record shows what happened next: criticism at home, a conference volume, and no specialist adoption.
open_questions: What Helskog actually concludes in 2014 about Caspian-Scandinavia boat resemblance. The chapter needs to be read in print (Novus, ISBN 978-82-7099-738-1, pp. 202-219) before the essay characterises his view. [uncertain]

Whether anyone has counted how many Gobustan boats carry a sun-prow or an upcurved end. Sigari gives examples by rock, not a frequency; 'common' rests on his word 'characteristically' and on 'recurrent' in the 2025 paper.
What Heyerdahl's second Gobustan boat type was.
Which year Heyerdahl first saw Gobustan (1980, 1981 and 1989 all appear).
What Farajova's chapter 'Boats in Rock Art of Gobustan' in the same volume says about types.
Whether the 'raised terminal' in the Ragazas article is the sun-prow or something else; the readable part of that article does not say.
